title: You’re Allowed to Want to Be Rich | Vivian Tu, Your Rich BFF
guest: Vivian Tu, founder of Your Rich BFF, former JP Morgan trader and BuzzFeed employee, author of Rich AF and Well Endowed
summary: Vivian Tu joins the hosts to talk about building wealth through downturns, recession-proofing your career, and why women must stop apologizing for wanting money. She shares tactical scripts for saying no to expensive bridesmaid duties, her $25 million FU number and how to calculate your own, her cost-benefit take on cars and homeownership, and the difference between looking rich and being rich.

ideas.idea: You will see five to eight major economic downturns in your adult life, and being ready with capital to deploy in each one can be the difference between being OK and being very comfortable.
ideas.detail: In March 2020 everyone was selling while rich people bought on the way down and kept buying; the market rebounded by August and the S&P 500 has since returned roughly 25% a year, rivaling private investments. The precondition is that the rest of your finances are safe first, and downturn bargains like secondhand designer goods or travel deals may not rebound like the index.

ideas.idea: It is not technically a recession (two quarters of negative GDP) but it is a 'vibecession' driven by a K-shaped economy where the rich get richer and everyone else feels squeezed.
ideas.detail: Regular people feel it at the grocery store, gas pump and in rent even without a technical downturn.

ideas.idea: Never try to call the bottom; invest a fixed dollar amount every month so you automatically buy fewer shares when prices are high and more when they are low.
ideas.detail: Even the smartest guys on Wall Street do not know where the bottom is; if she knew she would be retired. On a clearly major drop or rise you can decide to buy more or pause, but the default is to invest all the time.

ideas.idea: Loss aversion makes a $100 loss hurt more than a $100 gain feels good, so avoid checking your portfolio when the market is down and stay the course.
ideas.detail: She admits checking her own portfolio on a down day and having to laugh and take her own advice. The hosts propose a women's financial group chat as emotional support to buy rather than panic, since men effectively have one on Reddit.

ideas.idea: Recession-proof your career by choosing a role that transfers across industries, like accounting, marketing or software engineering, and by deciding whether you want growth or consistency.
ideas.detail: Healthcare, energy, utilities and staples hold up while discretionary sectors like movies and apparel get cut. If you are single you might chase rocket-ship growth, but a head of household feeding others may want to pivot toward stable industries with smaller raises. 'Accountants rise up.'

ideas.idea: 'Gold digger' is a tool to keep women down; every decision in life is a transaction and nobody calls men 'looks diggers' for the other side of the deal.
ideas.detail: Ambitious women get called power hungry, assertive women get called bossy, and no man has ever been called bossy, only a boss. Women should be loud about wanting financial stability, and she avoids relying on a man for money because whoever has the power to feed you has the power to starve you.

ideas.idea: Unbrainwash yourself with a daily mirror conversation: every dollar you made you earned, you are paid market rate, you are the only person who can do what you do, and you owe nobody anything.
ideas.detail: She reminds herself each morning that 'only good things happen to lucky girls like you' and that she now has what she dreamed of five years ago.

ideas.idea: Stop believing there is only room for one woman at the top; do not fight over crumbs, demand a bigger slice of the pie.
ideas.detail: On her JP Morgan trading desk the only other woman was her manager, 16 years her senior, alongside 30-40 white guys, and a new woman was hired only as one got senior. Women need to talk openly about pay, spending and what they pay employees, which gives everyone power. The hosts add their goal is not parity but an all-women top ten podcast chart.

ideas.idea: Friends who commiserate when you are down but go silent when you win are seeing a mirror of the work they did not do; cut frenemies and judge your success by whether you cheer for yourself.
ideas.detail: Responding to the hosts' loss of peer support after leaving corporate jobs, she asks herself daily whether she is proud of her work. Real friends' reactions, like a friend's mom texting after a TV appearance, show who truly wants the best for you; she has kept the same five college friends and now picks up dinners and flew last-minute to Vegas for a lonely friend.

ideas.idea: Before agreeing to be a bridesmaid, ask whether you would be comfortable Venmoing this person $5,000; if not, attend as a guest instead.
ideas.detail: Dress, shoes, flights, hotel plus engagement party, bachelorette and shower add up to thousands. Her script: congratulate, state your budget and constraints candidly, say you do not want to limit their moments, and ask what to prioritize or offer to support in other ways; the bride can then say skip the engagement party, offer to cover costs, or invite you as a guest.

ideas.idea: The red thread in money conversations with friends is not money but whether they love you; a bride who goes bridezilla over a budget never loved the friend, only being a show pony.
ideas.detail: These mature conversations require prep: the bridesmaid must actually know her budget rather than pulling a number from thin air.

ideas.idea: Run your bachelorette like user research: send an anonymous survey on dates, budget, vibe and location so no friend feels constrained by money.
ideas.detail: She sent a SurveyMonkey seen only by her because her friends range from pro bono attorneys to big-three consultants; every invitee later copied the survey for their own bachelorettes.

ideas.idea: Calculate your FU number by pricing your perfect year and dividing by 0.04; hers is $25 million invested, which throws off $1 million a year at a conservative 4% return.
ideas.detail: The $1 million covers a mortgage in a high-cost metro, private school for two kids, a full-time NYC nanny at roughly $135,000 with benefits, vacations, supporting her parents and taxes. Count only assets that actively throw off gains, not a house you would have to borrow against.

ideas.idea: A visible target keeps you going: like never hiding the Peloton progress bar, knowing exactly how far you have left to run toward your number is motivating.
ideas.detail: She compares it to a trainer telling her whether the set is 12 or 15 reps and Barry's counting down 60 seconds; if you are someone who swipes away the tracker this benchmarking may not help you.

ideas.idea: Your car is not an investment: it loses 10% the moment you drive off the lot and can be worth half its price by year five.
ideas.detail: Only rare supercars like the six McLarens made this year appreciate; nobody is dying for your base-model Lexus. She has no car in Miami, running a cost-benefit on lease, insurance, gas, maintenance versus Ubering, and notes rain is a free car wash.

ideas.idea: Lease, buy or rideshare depends on your use case: lease for job-transfer flexibility, buy the minivan you will drive into the ground, Uber if you are a hermit who goes out to drink.
ideas.detail: A friend in Texas leased because he might be transferred to LA, New York or London; Jean returned a three-year lease with under 5,000 miles. There is no perfect answer for everybody.

ideas.idea: You do not have to own a home to be doing well financially; a house only makes sense if you will stay at least five to seven years to amortize closing costs.
ideas.detail: People buy too small and then have three kids, or get a job elsewhere; property taxes, HOA or common charges and maintenance add up, like her $10,000 HVAC repair after a Japan trip. Homeownership can be part of your American dream but does not have to be.

ideas.idea: Immigrant parents often confuse looking rich (multiple cars and houses) with being rich; the billionaires she has met follow no such rules about what wealth means.
ideas.detail: Responding to the hosts' mom doubting they are doing well without multiple houses, she says truly wealthy people define wealth however they want, but also challenges the hosts to ask why they feel comfortable loosening the purse strings given the opportunity cost early in a lucrative career.

ideas.idea: Time is the only thing you cannot buy more of, so spend on a daily housekeeper and food delivery rather than status objects like Birkins.
ideas.detail: In the 'would you rather' round she picks a daily cleaner over 10 Birkins and food delivery over avocado toast, timing DoorDash orders to arrive as her workout ends.

ideas.idea: Even after hitting your FU number, do not retire; downshift from things you say yes to for money toward volunteer work, free speaking and teaching financial literacy.
ideas.detail: She would choose working to 65 and being extremely wealthy over retiring at 40 modestly, because she would be bored; getting to do something rather than having to do it wakes you up differently. A pipe dream is building a financial literacy curriculum for New York public high schools.
